title: 22. Interview: LRU (Least Recently Used)
summary: Interview Q&A for LRU (Least Recently Used) — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 LRU (Least Recently Used) interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is LRU, and how does it achieve O(1) per operation?
**Answer:** LRU (Least Recently Used) is a cache eviction policy that removes the entry accessed least recently when the cache is full. The intuition is temporal locality: recently accessed keys are likely to be re-accessed soon. LRU achieves O(1) per operation by combining two data structures: (1) a **hashmap** that maps each key to its linked-list node, providing O(1) lookup; (2) a **doubly-linked list** ordered by recency (most recent at the head, least recent at the tail), providing O(1) reordering given the node pointer. On a get, the hashmap finds the node in O(1), and the node is moved to the head in O(1) by updating four pointers (prev/next on the node and its neighbors). On a put that requires eviction, the tail node is removed in O(1) and the new node is inserted at the head in O(1). The space overhead is two pointers per entry (prev, next) plus the hashmap entry — typically 16–24 bytes per cached entry. Real-world: Python's `functools.lru_cache` uses `OrderedDict` (which is internally a hashmap + doubly-linked list); Redis uses an approximate LRU (sampling) for lock-free concurrency.
**Visual:**
```
Hashmap:                  Doubly-linked list (recency):
  key -> node pointer      HEAD <-> nodeA <-> nodeB <-> nodeC <-> TAIL
                           (most recent)                (least recent)

Get("A"):
  1. hashmap["A"] -> nodeA         O(1)
  2. move nodeA to HEAD            O(1) (4 pointer updates)
  3. return valueA

Put("D") on full cache:
  1. evict TAIL (nodeC)            O(1)
  2. insert nodeD at HEAD          O(1)
```

### Q2. Why does LRU use a doubly-linked list instead of a singly-linked list or an array?
**Answer:** A doubly-linked list is required because LRU needs to remove an arbitrary node (the accessed node, to move it to the head) in O(1) — given only the node pointer (from the hashmap). In a singly-linked list, removing an arbitrary node requires knowing its predecessor, which means walking the list from the head — O(n). In a doubly-linked list, the node has a `prev` pointer, so we can update `node.prev.next = node.next` and `node.next.prev = node.prev` in O(1) without walking. An array (or Python list) doesn't work because removing an arbitrary element is O(n) (shifting subsequent elements), and even with a "swap with last" trick, the recency order would be destroyed. The doubly-linked list is the canonical choice because it supports O(1) insertion at head, O(1) removal of the tail, and O(1) removal of an arbitrary node given its pointer — all the operations LRU needs. Real-world: every textbook LRU implementation uses a hashmap + doubly-linked list; Python's `OrderedDict` uses a similar structure internally (a hashmap + a doubly-linked list of keys).
**Visual:**
```
Doubly-linked list (O(1) removal of arbitrary node):
  ... <-> [P] <-> [NODE] <-> [Q] <-> ...
  remove NODE:
    P.next = Q      (1 pointer update)
    Q.prev = P      (1 pointer update)
  -> O(1), no walking needed

Singly-linked list (O(n) removal of arbitrary node):
  ... -> [P] -> [NODE] -> [Q] -> ...
  remove NODE:
    must find P first (walk from head) -> O(n)
    then P.next = Q
  -> O(n), unacceptable for cache hot path
```

### Q3. What is scan pollution, and why is LRU vulnerable to it?
**Answer:** Scan pollution occurs when a sequential read of cold keys displaces the hot working set from the cache. LRU is vulnerable because every access (even a one-time scan read) updates recency — each scanned key is "more recently used" than the previous hot keys, so the scan evicts hot keys to make room. After a scan of N keys (where N >= cache size), the cache holds the last N scanned keys (all cold) and 0 hot keys. Example: a 1000-entry cache with a 100-key hot set at 95% hit rate; a backup scans 5000 cold keys; the cache ends up with the last 1000 scanned keys (all cold); hit rate drops to 0% until the hot keys are re-accessed. The hot working set is effectively wiped by the scan. LFU and W-TinyLFU are scan-resistant because one-time scans don't accumulate enough frequency to evict high-frequency hot keys. LRU's lack of scan resistance is its main weakness, motivating variants like Segmented LRU, LRU-K, 2Q, and ARC. Real-world: a Redis cache with `allkeys-lru` will see hit rate collapse during nightly backups or crawls; operators switch to `allkeys-lfu` for scan-heavy workloads.
**Visual:**
```
Before scan: HEAD -> [H1][H2]...[H100] <- TAIL  (hot set resident, 95% hit)
Scan 100 cold keys (C1..C100):
  Each Ci inserted at HEAD, pushes hot toward TAIL
After scan:  HEAD -> [C100][C99]...[C1] <- TAIL  (hot set evicted, 0% hit)

Next access to H1 -> MISS (cache polluted by scan)
Hot set must be re-loaded -> hit rate stays low until re-warm

LRU is NOT scan-resistant (LFU and W-TinyLFU are)
```

### Q4. What is Segmented LRU, and how does it improve scan resistance?
**Answer:** Segmented LRU divides the cache into two segments: a **probationary segment** (new admissions) and a **protected segment** (entries accessed multiple times). New entries are admitted to the probationary segment; on a second access, they're promoted to the protected segment. Eviction happens from the probationary segment first (only when probationary is full); the protected segment is only evicted when it itself overflows (and then evicted entries go back to probationary, not out of the cache). The benefit for scan resistance: a one-time scan populates the probationary segment but doesn't touch the protected segment — the hot working set (which has been accessed multiple times) stays in protected, immune to scan pollution. The scan-evicted probationary entries are simply overwritten by the next scan or new admissions. This gives much of the scan resistance of LFU while keeping LRU's recency-based adaptation. Real-world: Caffeine uses a segmented design (window + probationary + protected); Memcached uses a similar segmented LRU since version 1.4.x; the Linux kernel's page cache uses active/inactive lists (a two-segment LRU). Segmented LRU is the simplest scan-resistant improvement over plain LRU.
**Visual:**
```
Plain LRU:
  HEAD -> [all entries in one list] <- TAIL
  scan evicts hot keys (no protection)

Segmented LRU:
  Probationary (new admissions, evicted first):
    HEAD -> [P1][P2]...[Pn] <- TAIL
  Protected (accessed 2+ times, evicted last):
    HEAD -> [H1][H2]...[Hm] <- TAIL

Scan of cold keys:
  + cold keys enter probationary
  + protected (hot) keys stay resident (not evicted)
  + probationary entries overwritten by next scan/admission

Result: hot set survives scans (scan-resistant)
```

### Q5. How does Redis implement LRU, and why doesn't it use a true global LRU list?
**Answer:** Redis implements **approximate LRU** via sampling: when `maxmemory` is reached and a write arrives, Redis samples N keys (controlled by `maxmemory-samples`, default 5) and evicts the least recently used among the sample. Redis doesn't maintain a true global LRU list (a doubly-linked list updated on every access) because: (1) **Lock contention** — a global list updated on every access would serialize all operations, killing Redis's single-threaded throughput (hundreds of thousands of ops/sec). (2) **Memory overhead** — a global list requires two pointers per entry (prev, next), which is significant when caching millions of small values. (3) **Implementation complexity** — maintaining the list correctly under Redis's various data structures (strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets) is non-trivial. The approximate LRU is within ~5% of true LRU's hit rate (at `maxmemory-samples 5`) and avoids all three costs. Operators can bump `maxmemory-samples` to 10 for closer-to-true LRU behavior at higher CPU cost. Redis 4.0+ also offers an approximate LFU mode using a similar sampling approach. Real-world: most production Redis deployments use the default `maxmemory-samples 5`; the trade-off is well-documented in `redis.conf`.
**Visual:**
```
True LRU:        global list, move-to-head on every access
                 + lock contention, 2 pointers/entry overhead
                 + exact LRU order

Redis approximate LRU:  sample N=5 keys, evict LRU among sample
                       + no global list, no lock contention
                       + ~5% hit-rate deviation from true LRU
                       + tunable: maxmemory-samples 10 (closer, more CPU)

maxmemory-samples=5  -> ~95% of true LRU hit rate
maxmemory-samples=10 -> ~98% of true LRU hit rate
```

### Q6. How does LRU compare to LFU? When does each win?
**Answer:** LRU evicts the entry accessed least recently (recency-based); LFU evicts the entry with the lowest access count (frequency-based). LRU wins on: (1) **Temporal-locality workloads** — recently accessed keys are likely to be re-accessed soon (session data, recently-viewed lists). (2) **Shifting hot sets** — LRU adapts within a few cache-misses; LFU adapts slowly because old counts persist. (3) **Implementation simplicity** — LRU is simpler (hashmap + linked list) than LFU (hashmap + min-heap or frequency buckets). LFU wins on: (1) **Stable hot sets** — frequency is a stronger signal than recency when the hot set is stable (popular products, trending videos). (2) **Scan-heavy workloads** — LFU is scan-resistant (one-time scans don't accumulate enough count); LRU is demolished by scans. (3) **Zipf-distributed workloads** — LFU typically achieves 2–5% higher hit rate than LRU on Zipf workloads because the hot keys' high counts protect them. The modern consensus: use W-TinyLFU (which combines recency and frequency) when implementation complexity is acceptable; use LRU as a safe default when simplicity matters; use LFU for stable-hot-set workloads with scans. Real-world: Redis recommends `allkeys-lru` for general, `allkeys-lfu` for stable hot keys with scans.
**Visual:**
```
Workload                  LRU  LFU  Winner
------------------------  ---  ---  ------
temporal locality         90%  85%  LRU (recent predicts future)
shifting hot set          85%  70%  LRU (adapts fast)
stable hot set, no scans  88%  92%  LFU (freq is strong signal)
scan-heavy                55%  90%  LFU (scan-resistant)
Zipf (typical web)        75%  80%  LFU (slight edge)
mixed (real-world)        78%  80%  W-TinyLFU (best of both)
```

### Q7. What are the concurrency challenges of LRU in multi-threaded caches, and how are they solved?
**Answer:** The doubly-linked list is a shared mutable structure — every access moves a node to the head, requiring updates to multiple pointers under a lock. In a multi-threaded cache, the lock becomes a bottleneck at high throughput (many threads contending on the same lock serializes operations). Solutions: (1) **Segmented LRU with per-segment locks** — divide keys across N segments (by hash), each with its own LRU list and lock; concurrent accesses to different segments don't contend; throughput scales with N. (2) **Approximate LRU** (Redis's approach) — don't maintain a global list; on eviction, sample N keys and pick the LRU among the sample; no lock contention on access, only on eviction. (3) **Lock-free LRU** — use CAS (compare-and-swap) operations on the linked list; complex but extremely high throughput; Caffeine uses a non-blocking design with a windowed TinyLFU admission. (4) **Sharded caches** — run multiple cache instances, each single-threaded (Redis's model); the client hashes the key to the right instance; no shared state, no locks. Each approach trades off complexity, hit-rate accuracy, and throughput. Real-world: Redis uses single-threaded per-instance (option 4) plus approximate LRU (option 2) — no locks at all within an instance; Caffeine uses lock-free design (option 3) for in-process Java caches; Memcached uses per-slab locks (option 1).
**Visual:**
```
Problem: global LRU list -> lock contention
  Thread1: get(A) -> lock -> move A to head -> unlock
  Thread2: get(B) -> wait for lock -> ...
  -> serialization kills throughput

Solutions:
  + segmented LRU (per-segment locks, hash-partitioned)
  + approximate LRU (sample N, no global list)
  + lock-free (CAS on linked list, Caffeine)
  + sharded caches (multiple instances, hash-routed)

Redis:     single-threaded per instance + approximate LRU (no locks)
Caffeine:  lock-free + W-TinyLFU admission
Memcached: per-slab locks + segmented LRU
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You're building an in-process cache for a Java service using Caffeine. The default is W-TinyLFU, but a teammate suggests switching to plain LRU for "simplicity." When is plain LRU the right choice?
**Answer:** Plain LRU is rarely the right choice in a modern cache library like Caffeine, because W-TinyLFU strictly dominates LRU on hit rate for almost all workloads (it adapts to both recency and frequency, and is scan-resistant). The only reasons to choose plain LRU: (1) **Predictability for debugging** — LRU's eviction order is deterministic and easy to reason about; if you're debugging a cache-related bug, plain LRU's behavior is easier to trace than W-TinyLFU's probabilistic sketch. (2) **Workload is purely temporal-locality with no scans and no stable hot set** — e.g., a session cache where the hot set shifts every few minutes and there are no scans; LRU's recency signal is exactly right, and W-TinyLFU's frequency tracking adds overhead without benefit. (3) **Memory overhead matters** — W-TinyLFU's Count-Min Sketch adds some memory overhead (typically 8–16 bytes per cached entry); for very small caches or memory-constrained environments, plain LRU is leaner. (4) **Latency sensitivity** — W-TinyLFU's sketch updates add a small constant to each access (typically nanoseconds); for ultra-low-latency caches (sub-microsecond), plain LRU might be marginally faster. In practice, none of these reasons are compelling for most applications — Caffeine's W-TinyLFU is the right default, and switching to plain LRU should require evidence that W-TinyLFU is hurting (which is rare). Real-world: Caffeine's documentation recommends W-TinyLFU for virtually all use cases.
**Visual:**
```
Plain LRU is right when:
  + debugging predictability needed (deterministic order)
  + pure temporal-locality workload (no scans, no stable hot)
  + memory-constrained (no sketch overhead)
  + ultra-low-latency (no sketch update overhead)

W-TinyLFU is right when (almost always):
  + scan-heavy workloads
  + stable hot sets
  + mixed workloads (real-world)
  + default for Caffeine, no reason to switch
```

### Q2. Your Redis cache uses `allkeys-lru` and has 1M entries. Hit rate is 80%. After a marketing email blast, hit rate drops to 40% for 10 minutes, then recovers. What happened, and how do you prevent it?
**Answer:** The marketing email blast drove a flood of users to the site, each accessing their own profile (and possibly new content). The flood of accesses to **new keys** (new user profiles, new content IDs) evicted the existing hot working set via LRU, dropping hit rate. After 10 minutes, the new accesses settled into a new stable hot set (the most-engaged users from the email blast), and hit rate recovered. To prevent: (1) **Pre-warm the cache** before the email blast — identify the keys most likely to be accessed (e.g., the email recipients' profiles) and load them into the cache; this avoids the cold-start misses. (2) **Increase cache capacity** during the blast — auto-scale Redis to a larger instance (or add shards) for the duration; the larger cache absorbs the new keys without evicting the old hot set. (3) **Switch to `allkeys-lfu`** — LFU's frequency tracking protects the established hot set from being evicted by one-time new-user accesses; the new keys need to accumulate multiple accesses before they can evict the hot set. (4) **Use a segmented cache** — separate the "established hot set" cache from the "new users" cache, so the new users don't pollute the hot set. (5) **Accept the temporary drop** — 40% for 10 minutes may be acceptable depending on SLO; the recovery is automatic. Real-world: Netflix and Amazon pre-warm caches before major launches (new show, Prime Day); Reddit scales cache capacity during AMAs and viral events.
**Visual:**
```
Before email blast:
  cache: [established hot set, 1M entries]  hit rate: 80%

Email blast -> flood of new users accessing their profiles:
  + new keys (user profiles) flood the cache
  + LRU evicts established hot set to admit new keys
  + hit rate: 40% (mix of new-key misses + hot-set-evicted misses)

After 10 min: new hot set stabilizes (engaged users from blast)
  + hit rate recovers to ~80% (new working set resident)

Prevention:
  + pre-warm cache (load expected new keys before blast)
  + scale capacity (larger cache absorbs burst)
  + switch to allkeys-lfu (hot set protected by frequency)
```

### Q3. You're implementing an LRU cache in Python for a service that handles 10K requests/sec. The naive single-lock implementation maxes out at 1K req/sec. How do you scale?
**Answer:** The single-lock LRU bottlenecks at ~1K req/sec because every access acquires the same lock, serializing all operations. To scale to 10K req/sec: (1) **Segmented LRU with per-segment locks** — divide keys across N segments (e.g., 16) by hash; each segment has its own LRU list and lock; concurrent accesses to different segments don't contend; throughput scales roughly with N (so 16 segments → ~16K req/sec). This is the simplest and most effective fix. (2) **Use `functools.lru_cache` per process** — if the service is multi-process (e.g., gunicorn with 8 workers), each process has its own LRU; total throughput is N_processes × per-process throughput (8 × 1K = 8K req/sec); doesn't quite hit 10K but close. (3) **Move to a dedicated cache process** — use Redis or Memcached (which handle 100K+ req/sec per instance via single-threaded event loop, no locks); the service makes a network call to the cache; the network round-trip (~0.5 ms) is acceptable if it replaces a 5 ms DB call. (4) **Lock-free LRU** — implement a CAS-based lock-free LRU in Python (using `threading` primitives); possible but complex and Python's GIL limits the benefit. (5) **Shard across multiple cache instances** — like option 3 but with multiple Redis/Memcached instances, hash-routed; scales linearly with instance count. For a Python service, option 1 (segmented LRU) is the easiest in-process fix; option 3 (dedicated cache) is the standard production choice. Real-world: most Python services at scale use Redis/Memcached, not in-process LRU, for exactly this reason.
**Visual:**
```
Single-lock LRU: 1K req/sec (lock contention)

Options to scale to 10K req/sec:
  + segmented LRU (16 segments, 16 locks) -> ~16K req/sec (in-process)
  + multi-process (8 workers × 1K)        -> 8K req/sec (close, in-process)
  + dedicated cache (Redis/Memcached)     -> 100K+ req/sec (network call)
  + sharded cache (multiple instances)    -> linear scaling

For Python service: segmented LRU is easiest in-process fix;
                   dedicated Redis is standard production choice.
```

### Q4. Your LRU cache has a 95% hit rate, but p99 latency is 50 ms while p50 is 0.5 ms. The cache itself is in-process (no network). What's causing the tail latency, and how do you fix it?
**Answer:** A 100x gap between p50 (0.5 ms) and p99 (50 ms) in an in-process LRU cache suggests infrequent but expensive operations on the cache hot path. Likely causes: (1) **Lazy cleanup or resize** — if the LRU uses lazy deletion (mark nodes as deleted, clean up periodically) or hash rebalancing (resize when load factor exceeds threshold), the cleanup/resize is O(n) and causes a latency spike when it runs. Fix: bound the cleanup work (clean up at most K nodes per operation) or use a pre-sized hashmap (no resize). (2) **GC pauses** — in a garbage-collected language (Java, Python, Go), creating many short-lived objects (LRU nodes) triggers GC pauses; the 50 ms p99 could be a GC pause. Fix: object pooling (reuse node objects), reduce allocation rate, or tune GC. (3) **Lock contention spike** — if a few operations hold the lock for a long time (e.g., a scan that touches many nodes), other operations queue behind them. Fix: segmented locks, or move long operations off the hot path. (4) **Eviction storm** — if many keys expire at the same TTL, a burst of evictions happens simultaneously, spiking latency. Fix: jitter TTLs (add random ±10% to spread expirations). (5) **OS-level interruptions** — page faults, context switches, or container CPU throttling can cause 50 ms spikes; check `top` and `perf` for evidence. Diagnose by adding per-operation timing and looking for correlations (does the spike happen during GC? during resize? during a particular request pattern?). Real-world: Java caches use `-XX:+UseG1GC` with low-pause targets; Python services use `gc.set_threshold` tuning or move to PyPy for lower GC overhead.
**Visual:**
```
p50=0.5ms, p99=50ms (100x gap) in in-process LRU:

Likely causes:
  + lazy cleanup / hash resize (O(n) spike)
  + GC pauses (object allocations)
  + lock contention spike (long operations)
  + eviction storm (simultaneous TTL expirations)
  + OS interruptions (page faults, throttling)

Diagnose:
  + per-operation timing
  + correlate spikes with GC log / resize events / TTL expirations

Fix:
  + bound cleanup (K nodes per op)
  + pre-size hashmap (no resize)
  + object pooling (reduce GC)
  + jitter TTLs (spread expirations)
  + segmented locks (reduce contention)
```

### Q5. You're using Python's `functools.lru_cache` to memoize a function. After a long-running batch job, you notice the cache has 10M entries and is consuming 8 GB of RAM. How do you bound it?
**Answer:** `functools.lru_cache` accepts a `maxsize` parameter that bounds the cache; the default is 128, but if you've explicitly set `maxsize=None` (unbounded) or a very large `maxsize`, the cache grows without limit. To bound it: (1) **Set `maxsize` to a reasonable value** — e.g., `@lru_cache(maxsize=100_000)`; this evicts the least recently used entries when the cache exceeds 100K, keeping memory bounded. Choose `maxsize` based on the expected hot working set size and available memory. (2) **Use `cache_clear()` periodically** — if the batch job processes distinct keys (no reuse), the cache provides no benefit; clear it periodically (e.g., every 100K calls) to free memory. (3) **Use `cache_info()` to monitor** — `functools.lru_cache` exposes `cache_info()` returning hits, misses, current size, and max size; check this to verify the cache is providing value (high hit rate) or not (low hit rate, should be cleared). (4) **Don't use `lru_cache` for batch jobs** — if the batch job processes each key once with no reuse, memoization provides no benefit; remove the decorator. (5) **Switch to a TTL-based cache** — if entries are useful only for a short time, use `cachetools.TTLCache` or `expiringdict` instead of `lru_cache`; entries auto-expire after a TTL, bounding memory. (6) **Use weak references** — `functools.lru_cache` doesn't support weak refs, but `WeakValueDictionary`-based caches allow garbage collection of entries when no other references exist. Real-world: `lru_cache` is great for in-process memoization of pure functions but should always have a `maxsize` set; unbounded caches are a common source of memory leaks in Python services.
**Visual:**
```
functools.lru_cache(maxsize=None) -> unbounded -> 10M entries, 8GB RAM (leak)

Fix:
  + set maxsize (e.g., maxsize=100_000) -> bounded LRU eviction
  + cache_clear() periodically (if no reuse, no benefit)
  + check cache_info() (hits/misses/size) to verify value
  + remove decorator (if batch has no reuse)
  + use TTLCache (if entries useful only briefly)
  + use weak refs (if other refs determine lifetime)

Always set maxsize on lru_cache in production.
```

### Q6. Your team is debating LRU vs LFU for a Netflix-style "continue watching" list. Users return to shows they were watching recently, but a small set of popular shows dominates. Which do you choose?
**Answer:** This is a workload with **both temporal locality (recently-watched predicts next-watch) and a stable hot set (popular shows)** — both signals are useful. LRU captures temporal locality (recently-watched shows stay resident), which is the stronger signal for "continue watching" specifically — a user who paused a show 10 minutes ago is very likely to resume it. LFU captures the stable hot set (popular shows), but for "continue watching," the hot set is per-user (each user has their own continue-watching list), so a global LFU doesn't help as much. The best choice depends on the cache scope: (1) **Per-user cache** (each user has their own LRU of recently-watched) — LRU is exactly right; the user's most recently watched show is at the head, ready to resume. (2) **Global cache** (one cache shared across all users, keying by show ID) — LFU or W-TinyLFU is better; popular shows are accessed by many users and should stay resident. (3) **Hybrid** (per-user LRU for the continue-watching list, global LFU for show metadata) — the best of both; the per-user LRU captures the user's personal recency, and the global LFU caches popular show metadata (thumbnails, descriptions) efficiently. Real-world: Netflix uses per-user session state (LRU-like) for continue-watching, and a global cache (LFU-like) for show metadata; the two serve different purposes. For your team, if the cache is per-user, use LRU; if global, use W-TinyLFU; if you can split, do both.
**Visual:**
```
"Continue watching" workload:
  + per-user: recently-watched predicts next-watch (temporal locality)
  + global:   popular shows dominate (stable hot set)

Per-user cache (each user's continue-watching list):
  + LRU is exactly right (most recent at head, ready to resume)
  + LFU doesn't help (each user's list is small, freq tracking redundant)

Global cache (show metadata, thumbnails):
  + LFU or W-TinyLFU (popular shows stay resident)
  + LRU works but loses ~5% hit rate vs LFU

Hybrid (best):
  + per-user LRU for continue-watching
  + global LFU/W-TinyLFU for show metadata
```

### Q7. Your LRU cache evicts a hot key during a brief traffic spike, causing a thundering herd of DB queries. How do you prevent this?
**Answer:** When a hot key is evicted, the next request misses and queries the DB; if many requests arrive simultaneously (traffic spike), they all miss and all query the DB — a **thundering herd** (also called cache stampede). Preventing this requires protecting the hot key from eviction AND preventing simultaneous misses. Solutions: (1) **Per-key locks (request coalescing)** — when a miss occurs, acquire a per-key lock; only the first request queries the DB and populates the cache; subsequent requests wait for the lock, then read from the cache. This prevents the stampede even if the key is evicted. (2) **Hot key pinning** — identify hot keys (high access rate) and pin them in the cache (mark as non-evictable); they bypass LRU eviction. (3) **Soft TTL with early refresh** — set a TTL but refresh the cache slightly before expiry (e.g., at 80% of TTL), so the refresh happens off the hot path; this prevents the miss that triggers the stampede. (4) **Probabilistic early expiration** — each request, with a small probability p, refreshes the cache before expiry; this spreads the refresh across requests, avoiding a synchronized miss. (5) **Two-layer cache** — a small "hot key" cache (LFU, never evicted) plus a larger "general" cache (LRU); hot keys live in the hot cache and don't get evicted by LRU. (6) **Increase cache size** — if hot keys are being evicted due to undersized cache, simply size up. Real-world: Netflix uses per-key locks (request coalescing) on EVCache; Redis has no built-in coalescing, but application-level locks (e.g., Redlock per key) achieve the same effect. Caffeine supports `AsyncCache` which coalesces concurrent loads of the same key.
**Visual:**
```
Hot key evicted during traffic spike:
  T=0: hot key H evicted by LRU
  T=1ms: 100 requests for H arrive simultaneously
         -> all miss -> 100 DB queries -> DB overloaded (stampede)

Prevention:
  + per-key locks: first miss acquires lock, others wait, then read cache
                   -> 1 DB query, 99 cache reads
  + hot key pinning: H never evicted (bypass LRU)
  + soft TTL + early refresh: refresh before expiry, no miss
  + probabilistic early expiration: spread refresh across requests
  + two-layer cache: hot cache (LFU) + general cache (LRU)

Best practice: per-key locks + hot key pinning (defense in depth)
```

quiz.explanation: Scan pollution occurs when a sequential read of cold keys displaces the hot working set from the cache. LRU is vulnerable because every access (even a one-time scan read) updates recency — each scanned key is "more recently used" than the previous hot keys, so the scan evicts hot keys to make room. After a scan of N keys (where N >= cache size), the cache holds the last N scanned keys (all cold) and 0 hot keys.

quiz.explanation: Segmented LRU divides the cache into two segments: a probationary segment (new admissions) and a protected segment (entries accessed multiple times). New entries are admitted to the probationary segment; on a second access, they're promoted to the protected segment.
